mainTopic: The end of יאשיהו's story, and the משנה's cases of fasting and crying out: blight, wolves, dangers on שבת, plague, and too much rain.
overview: The גמרא finishes the story of יאשיהו. He fought פרעה נכה because he read the פסוק 'a sword shall not pass through your land' as including even a peaceful army. He did not ask ירמיהו and did not realize his generation was unworthy, and he died accepting God's judgment. The גמרא then returns to the משנה. It asks how much blight 'fills the mouth of an oven' (תיקו), and it tells of wolves that swallowed children, whose digested flesh was ruled טהור and whose bones were ruled טמא. A ברייתא lists dangers for which an alarm is sounded on שבת. רבי יוסי argues that an individual may not weaken himself by fasting. The גמרא shows that the חכמים never cry out over plague. Finally, no alarm is sounded for too much rain, since we do not pray against too much good, except in the גולה. רבי אליעזר's measure for praying against rain and a ברייתא about moderate rain close the amud.

steps.title: פרעה נכה's message to יאשיהו
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק where פרעה נכה tells יאשיהו that he is not fighting him and warns him not to interfere.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pharaoh sent messengers to יאשיהו: 'What do you have to do with me, king of יהודה? I am not coming to fight you today. I am fighting a different nation, and God told me to hurry. Stop interfering with the God who is with me, so He will not destroy you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק from דברי הימים to set up the next question. Pharaoh is telling יאשיהו to stay out of the fight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק shows that Pharaoh had no plan to attack יאשיהו's kingdom. So the battle was something יאשיהו chose. The words 'אלהים אשר עמי' are unclear, and the גמרא will ask about them next.

keyTerms.meaning: The nation I am at war with

phrases.english: "And he sent messengers to him, saying:
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 35:21. 'He' is פרעה נכה, king of מצרים.

phrases.english: What have I to do with you, king of Judah?
Not against you do I come this day,
but against the house with which I am at war;
and God has told me to hurry.
Stop interfering with God, Who is with me,
so that He will not destroy you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ongoing story of יאשיהו from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pharaoh told יאשיהו that he was not his target and warned him not to interfere.

steps.title: Which 'God' did Pharaoh mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what Pharaoh meant by 'the God Who is with me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'God Who is with me' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about one phrase in the פסוק. This sets up רב's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It sounds strange for a non-Jewish king to say ה׳ is with him. The גמרא wants to know what he really meant.

keyTerms.meaning: The god that is with me

phrases.english: What is the meaning of "God, Who is with me"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a phrase in the פסוק quoted in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who or what Pharaoh meant by 'the God who is with me.'

steps.title: It was עבודה זרה, so יאשיהו felt sure he would win
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that Pharaoh meant his עבודה זרה. יאשיהו reasoned that someone who trusts in idols can be defeated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: This means his idol. יאשיהו said: Since he trusts in an idol, I can beat him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question: the 'god' was Pharaoh's idol. Then the גמרא tells us how יאשיהו reacted to that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'אלהים' is not ה׳'s name; it means a false god. This explains why יאשיהו ignored the warning: he thought a king who relies on idols could not succeed against him.

keyTerms.meaning: Idol worship; here, the idol itself

steps.confusionAlert: The word אמר ('he said') in the second half is יאשיהו speaking, not רב.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
This is idolatry.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: הוֹאִיל וְקָא בָּטַח בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה —
phrases.english: He said: Since he trusts in idolatry,
phrases.notes: 'He' here is יאשיהו, explaining to himself why he went to fight.

phrases.english: I can defeat him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב זוֹ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'god' was Pharaoh's idol, which made יאשיהו confident he could win.

steps.title: What does 'I am badly wounded' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about the archers shooting יאשיהו and asks what 'very wounded' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The archers shot at King יאשיהו, and the king told his servants: 'Take me away, for I am very wounded.' What does 'very wounded' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the story and asks about one phrase. This sets up רב's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'מאד' (very) seems to be telling us how badly he was hurt. The גמרא wants to know exactly what it describes.

phrases.english: "And the archers shot at King Josiah,
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 35:23.

phrases.english: and the king said to his servants:
Take me away, for I am very wounded."
What is the meaning of "for I am very wounded"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves forward in the story to the battle itself.

steps.title: His body was pierced like a sieve
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the arrows made יאשיהו's whole body full of holes, like a sieve.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: This teaches that they made his whole body like a sieve.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question: 'very wounded' means he was hit by so many arrows that his body was full of holes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'מאד' tells us the wounds were extreme. This shows how harsh יאשיהו's punishment was, which leads into the next step asking why he was punished.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
This teaches that they made his whole body like a sieve.
phrases.notes: From all the arrows the archers shot at him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His whole body was pierced by arrows like a sieve.

steps.title: יאשיהו was punished for not consulting ירמיהו
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני says in the name of רבי יונתן that יאשיהו was punished because he did not ask ירמיהו הנביא before going to war.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Why was יאשיהו punished? Because he should have asked ירמיהו, and he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement explains the reason for יאשיהו's terrible death. He went to war without asking the נביא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יאשיהו was a righteous king, so his death needs a reason. The answer is not a sin of idol worship. It is that he decided on war on his own, when a נביא was available to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: The נביא ירמיהו, who lived in יאשיהו's time

steps.whatToRemember: יאשיהו's mistake was acting without asking the נביא, even though his intentions were good.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
For what reason was Josiah punished?
Because he should have consulted Jeremiah,
and he did not consult him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After describing his death, the גמרא explains why it happened.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יאשיהו was punished for not consulting ירמיהו before the war.

steps.title: Which פסוק led יאשיהו to go to war
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what יאשיהו learned that made him go to war, and begins the answer with the פסוק 'and a sword shall not pass through your land.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What did he learn from the פסוקים? 'And a sword shall not pass through your land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what reasoning made יאשיהו feel safe going to war. It starts to answer by quoting a פסוק, and steps 8-10 finish the explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יאשיהו did not act without thinking; he relied on a promise from the תורה. He read it as saying that no army, not even a peaceful one, would pass through a righteous land. So he set out to stop Pharaoh.

keyTerms.meaning: What did he learn from the פסוק
And a sword shall not pass

phrases.english: What did he expound?
"And a sword shall not pass through your land."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 26:6.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what led to the mistake described in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק and reading led יאשיהו to fight Pharaoh.

steps.title: What kind of 'sword' does the verse mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'sword' means in the פסוק יאשיהו relied on. It rejects the idea that it means a hostile sword, because the same פסוק already promised peace.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'sword' mean here? If you say it means a sword that is not peaceful (an attacking army), that can't be right, because the same verse already says 'I will give peace in the land'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is working out exactly what יאשיהו learned from the פסוק. It first tries one meaning of 'sword' and knocks it down, which sets up the real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'sword' meant enemy attack, the words 'a sword shall not pass' would add nothing, since 'I will give peace in the land' already promises there will be no war. So 'sword' must mean something beyond an enemy attack.

keyTerms.meaning: Sword; here it stands for an army
If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
But isn't it written (introduces a verse that challenges the suggestion)

phrases.english: What is meant by "sword"?
If you say it means a sword that is not of peace,
but isn't it written: "And I will give peace in the land"!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 26:6. This is the same פסוק that goes on to say 'a sword shall not pass through your land.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues step 7 by defining the key word of the פסוק יאשיהו relied on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of 'sword' the פסוק promises will not pass through the land.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'sword' means an enemy attack.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier words 'I will give peace in the land' already cover that, so the extra phrase would add nothing.

steps.title: Even a peaceful army is included
steps.stepSummary: The 'sword' means even a sword 'of peace,' an army just passing through. That is why יאשיהו tried to stop פרעה from crossing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means even a sword of peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real meaning: the blessing promises that not even a non-hostile army will cross the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרעה was not attacking יהודה. He only wanted to pass through. יאשיהו understood the blessing to mean that even this should not happen, so he went out to stop it.

phrases.english: Rather, it means even a sword of peace.
phrases.notes: A 'sword of peace' is an army that is just marching through, not fighting you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8 after the first meaning was rejected.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Sword' includes even a peaceful army passing through, so יאשיהו tried to block פרעה.

steps.title: יאשיהו's mistake: his generation was not worthy
steps.stepSummary: יאשיהו did not realize that his generation did not deserve the blessing of the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he did not know that his generation was not worthy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains where יאשיהו went wrong. His reading of the פסוק was correct, but the blessing depends on the people deserving it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The blessings in this part of ויקרא are promised to those who keep the תורה. Since his generation did not merit them, he could not count on the protection. This ties back to step 6: had he asked ירמיהו, he would have found out.

keyTerms.meaning: Looks good, meaning worthy or deserving

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows why asking ירמיהו (step 6) mattered: knowing the פסוק was not enough without knowing whether the generation deserved it.

phrases.english: But he did not know
that his generation was not worthy.
phrases.notes: Literally 'his generation does not look nice,' meaning it did not deserve the blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהוּא אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין דּוֹרוֹ דּוֹמֶה יָפֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the reading from step 9 still led to disaster.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יאשיהו's reading was right, but his generation did not merit the blessing.

steps.title: ירמיהו worries about יאשיהו's last words
steps.stepSummary: As יאשיהו lay dying, ירמיהו saw his lips moving and feared he might be complaining against ה׳ because of his pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: When יאשיהו was dying, ירמיהו saw his lips moving. He said: Perhaps, heaven forbid, he is saying something improper because of his pain.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to יאשיהו's death. This step sets up the scene: ירמיהו is afraid of what the king might be saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person in great suffering might speak against God's judgment. ירמיהו's worry builds tension that the next step resolves.

phrases.english: When he was dying,
Jeremiah saw his lips moving,
he said: Perhaps, heaven forbid,
he is saying something improper
because of his suffering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the wounding in step 5 and the explanation of his mistake, the story moves to יאשיהו's final moments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ירמיהו feared that the dying יאשיהו was complaining about God's judgment.

steps.title: יאשיהו accepts God's judgment and ירמיהו eulogizes him
steps.stepSummary: ירמיהו leaned in and heard יאשיהו declaring that ה׳ is righteous and that he himself had sinned. ירמיהו then began his eulogy, 'The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of ה׳.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He bent down and heard that he was accepting the judgment on himself as fair. He was saying: 'ה׳ is righteous, for I rebelled against His word.' At that moment ירמיהו began about him: 'The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The fear from the last step turns out to be wrong: יאשיהו was praising God's justice and blaming himself. This closes the story of יאשיהו with ירמיהו's eulogy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of complaining, יאשיהו admitted his mistake of not asking the prophet. Because of this, ירמיהו honored him as 'the breath of our nostrils,' showing he died a צדיק even though he had erred.

keyTerms.meaning: Accepting the judgment as just (צידוק הדין)
The anointed one of ה׳, meaning the king

steps.whatToRemember: יאשיהו went to war based on a correct reading of the פסוק, but he did not ask ירמיהו and did not know his generation was unworthy. At his death he accepted God's judgment, and ירמיהו eulogized him.

phrases.english: He bent down and heard him
accepting the judgment against himself as just;
he said: "The Lord is righteous,
for I have rebelled against His word."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:18

phrases.english: At that moment Jeremiah began about him:
phrases.notes: 'Began about him' means ירמיהו opened a eulogy for him.

phrases.english: "The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord."
phrases.notes: איכה 4:20

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּחֵין וְשַׁמְעֵיהּ דְּקָא מַצְדֵּיק עֲלֵיהּ דִּינָא אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves ירמיהו's worry from step 11 and closes the יאשיהו story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יאשיהו died accepting God's judgment, and ירמיהו honored him with a eulogy.

steps.title: How much blight is 'enough to fill an oven'?
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה about elders who declared a fast over a small amount of blight, the גמרא asks whether the amount means grain to fill an oven or bread to fill an oven.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'It happened that elders went down from ירושלים to their cities' and so on. They asked: Does it mean enough grain to fill an oven, or perhaps enough bread to fill an oven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the יאשיהו story and returns to the משנה. It asks what amount of damaged grain the משנה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Filling a whole oven with grain is a large amount. Bread only sticks to the oven walls, so the grain needed to make an oven's worth of bread is much less. The question is which measure the משנה means.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them (the חכמים)

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה וְיָרְדוּ זְקֵנִים מִירוּשָׁלַיִם לְעָרֵיהֶם כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: "An incident: elders went down from Jerusalem to their cities, etc."
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. They declared a fast because blight was seen on grain in אשקלון, enough to fill the mouth of an oven.

phrases.english: They asked:
enough grain to fill an oven,
or perhaps enough bread to fill an oven?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the משנה after the יאשיהו story ends.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the measure is an oven full of grain or an oven's load of bread.

steps.title: The משנה says 'the mouth of an oven'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from the exact wording: 'enough to fill the mouth of an oven.' This points to bread, the smaller amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: the משנה says 'enough to fill the mouth of an oven.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by looking closely at the words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grain would fill the whole oven, but the משנה only speaks of the 'mouth' (opening). That fits bread, which is placed around the top of the oven, not loose grain filling it.

phrases.english: Come and hear: "enough to fill the mouth of an oven."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 from the משנה's own wording.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'mouth' shows the measure is bread, not a whole oven full of grain.

steps.title: Which kind of 'mouth of the oven' amount?
steps.stepSummary: Even if it means bread, a new question remains: is it one loaf covering the opening, or a ring of loaves around the rim of the opening?
steps.simpleTranslation: And still they can ask: Is it like a loaf that covers the oven's opening, or perhaps like a row of loaves going around the mouth of the oven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the last answer but raises a smaller question about exactly how much bread is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Filling the mouth of an oven' could mean one flat loaf lying over the opening like a lid. Or it could mean a ring of loaves stuck all around the rim. These are different amounts.

keyTerms.meaning: And still the question can be asked

phrases.english: And still they can ask:
is it like the cover of the oven,
phrases.notes: He means a single loaf lying over the opening like a lid.

phrases.english: or perhaps like a row of loaves
that goes around the mouth of the oven?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 14's answer and asks a narrower follow-up question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'the mouth of an oven' means one covering loaf or a ring of loaves around the rim.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finds no answer, so the question is left standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends this discussion with no answer to the last question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first question (grain or bread) was answered, but the follow-up (lid-loaf or ring of loaves) was not. תיקו means the question remains open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The measure in the משנה is bread at the mouth of the oven, not a whole oven full of grain. Whether it means one covering loaf or a ring of loaves is left as תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes step 15's question with no resolution.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Which bread amount is meant remains undecided.

steps.title: Wolves swallowed two children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the fast declared after wolves ate children, and עולא reports what happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said they also declared a fast because wolves ate children. עולא, in the name of רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק, said: there was an incident where wolves swallowed two children and passed them out through their bodies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the next line of the משנה and gives the background story behind it. This sets up a halachic ruling that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only mentioned that wolves ate children. עולא adds a detail: the children's remains came out of the wolves' bodies. That detail matters because the חכמים will be asked about the טומאה of those remains.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident or story that really happened
The place where waste leaves the body

phrases.english: And furthermore, they decreed a fast
because wolves had eaten, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה. The כו׳ means "and so on": the משנה says two children were eaten.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר עוּלָּא מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק:
phrases.english: Ulla said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak:
There was an incident in which wolves swallowed two children
and expelled them through the excretory passage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר עולא משום רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the open question about the oven in step 16, the גמרא moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא reports the actual incident behind the משנה: wolves swallowed two children and expelled their remains.

steps.title: Flesh is pure, bones are impure
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ruled that the digested flesh was טהור but the bones were טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case came before the חכמים. They declared the flesh pure and the bones impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the חכמים' ruling on the טומאה of the children's remains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Flesh that has passed through an animal's digestion no longer counts as part of a dead body, so it is טהור. The bones came out whole, so they still carry the טומאה of a dead person.
steps.whatToRemember: Flesh digested by an animal becomes טהור, but bones that come out intact stay טמא.

phrases.english: And the incident came before the Sages,
and they declared the flesh ritually pure,
and declared the bones ritually impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story from step 17 with the halachic ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Digested flesh is טהור; intact bones remain טמא.

steps.title: Dangers that justify an alarm on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה on sounding an alarm on שבת and brings a ברייתא with a longer list of dangers.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: for these things an alarm is sounded on שבת. A ברייתא teaches: a city surrounded by enemies or by a flooding river, a ship in danger at sea, and an individual chased by enemies, bandits, or an evil spirit. For all of these, an alarm is sounded on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next part of the משנה and quotes a ברייתא that spells out which dangers allow sounding an alarm even on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed a city, a river, and a ship. The ברייתא adds something new: a single person in danger, whether from enemies, bandits, or an evil spirit. So even one person's danger is serious enough to cry out on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Sounding an alarm, crying out for help and prayer
A ship being tossed by a storm

phrases.english: For these they sound the alarm on Shabbat, etc.
The Rabbis taught:
A city that gentile troops or a river have surrounded,
and likewise a ship tossed about at sea,
and likewise an individual pursued by gentiles

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ מִפְּנֵי לִסְטִין וּמִפְּנֵי רוּחַ רָעָה
phrases.english: or by bandits or by an evil spirit
they sound the alarm on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: תנו רבנן עיר שהקיפוה נכרים או נהר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה about crying out on שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An alarm is sounded on שבת for a besieged or flooded city, a ship in distress, or an individual being chased.

steps.title: An individual may fast in these cases
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that in all these dangers an individual is allowed to fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: In all these cases, an individual is allowed to afflict himself with a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא continues and teaches that a person in any of these dangers may fast to pray for help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to here the ברייתא was about sounding an alarm. Now it adds a second rule: a private fast is allowed in these cases. This is the view of the תנא קמא, and רבי יוסי will argue against it next.

keyTerms.meaning: An individual, one person on his own
To afflict himself, to cause himself hardship

phrases.english: And in all of these cases,

phrases.aramaic: יָחִיד רַשַּׁאי לְסַגֵּף אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּתַעֲנִית.
phrases.english: an individual is permitted to afflict himself by fasting.

steps.triggerLanguage: ועל כולן יחיד רשאי לסגף את עצמו בתענית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second rule to the ברייתא from step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, an individual may fast in all of these dangers.

steps.title: רבי יוסי forbids an individual to fast
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says an individual may not afflict himself with fasting, because he may come to depend on others.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: an individual may not afflict himself with a fast. He might become weak and need help from other people, and they will not have mercy on him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי disagrees with the previous line of the ברייתא and says an individual should not fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is practical. Fasting can weaken a person until he cannot earn a living. Then he has to rely on other people, who may not help him. So רבי יוסי forbids the private fast.

keyTerms.meaning: He will need other people, come to depend on them

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
An individual is not permitted
to afflict himself by fasting,
lest he come to need other people
and people will not have mercy on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רבי יוסי אומר אין היחיד רשאי לסגף את עצמו בתענית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the rule in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An individual may not fast, since he may come to depend on others who will not help him.

steps.title: What is רבי יוסי's source?
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב asks for the reason behind רבי יוסי's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: what is רבי יוסי's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: רב asks for the source of רבי יוסי's view. This sets up the answer from a פסוק in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי already gave a practical reason. Asking "what is the reason" here means looking for a source in the תורה that backs his view.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Yosei?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב יהודה אמר רב מאי טעמא דרבי יוסי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for the source of רבי יוסי's view from step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for רבי יוסי's ban on an individual fasting.

steps.title: Keep alive the soul I gave you
steps.stepSummary: רב reads "and man became a living soul" as a command to keep one's soul alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "And man became a living soul." This means: the soul I gave you, keep it alive.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers with a פסוק that shows a person must take care of his own life and health.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes how man was created. רב reads it as an instruction: ה׳ gave you a living soul, so you must keep it strong. Weakening yourself by fasting goes against this.
steps.whyThisMatters: This דרשה is a well-known source for a person's duty to look after his own health.

phrases.english: As it is written: "And man became a living soul"
phrases.notes: בראשית 2:7

phrases.english: The soul that I placed in you, keep it alive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק "ויהי האדם לנפש חיה" is read as a command to sustain the soul ה׳ gave you.

steps.title: How far did the חכמים disagree with שמעון התימני?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the חכמים rejected crying out over plague only on שבת, or rejected it completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: שמעון התימני says we cry out even for a plague. The question was asked: did the חכמים disagree with him only about שבת, but agree that we cry out on a weekday? Or did they not agree with him at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and asks how far the חכמים' disagreement goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says only that the חכמים "did not agree" with שמעון התימני. That could mean they argued only about שבת, or that they hold no alarm is sounded for plague even on a weekday. The גמרא is asking which one.

keyTerms.meaning: "It was asked of them", an open question raised in the בית המדרש

phrases.english: Shimon the Timnite says:
Even for pestilence, etc.
A question was raised before them:
Did the Sages not agree with him only on Shabbat,
but on a weekday they agreed with him,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא: לֹא הוֹדוּ לוֹ כְּלָל?
phrases.english: or perhaps they did not agree with him at all?

steps.triggerLanguage: איבעיא להו לא הודו לו חכמים בשבת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה about שמעון התימני.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the חכמים rejected crying out over plague only on שבת or in all cases.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows a view that you never cry out over plague
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with two views. The first view says you cry out over plague even on שבת. רבי עקיבא holds you do not cry out over plague at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as a ברייתא teaches: We cry out over a plague even on שבת, and certainly on a weekday. רבי חנן בן פיטום, the student of רבי עקיבא, says in the name of רבי עקיבא: We do not cry out over a plague at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 24 by quoting a ברייתא. It shows there is a view that rejects crying out over plague completely, not only on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was whether the חכמים object to crying out over plague only on שבת, or at any time. The first view in the ברייתא matches שמעון התימני, and רבי עקיבא's view, that you never cry out over plague, matches the חכמים of the משנה. So the answer is that the חכמים did not agree with him at all, even on a weekday.

keyTerms.meaning: We cry out or sound the alarm (with prayer and the shofar or trumpets)
Plague, a deadly disease spreading in a town

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it is taught in a ברייתא:
We cry out over plague on שבת,
and needless to say on a weekday.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חָנָן בֶּן פִּיטוֹם תַּלְמִידוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
phrases.english: רבי חנן בן פיטום, the student of רבי עקיבא,
says in the name of רבי עקיבא:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מַתְרִיעִין עַל הַדֶּבֶר כׇּל עִיקָּר.
phrases.english: We do not cry out over plague at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים hold like רבי עקיבא in the ברייתא: they did not agree with שמעון התימני at all, and no alarm is sounded for plague even on a weekday.
steps.whatToRemember: One view: cry out over plague even on שבת. רבי עקיבא: never cry out over plague at all.

steps.title: Every trouble gets an alarm except too much rain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and a ברייתא: we sound the alarm for every trouble that may come on the community, except too much rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'For every trouble that should not come upon the community...' The רבנן taught in a ברייתא: For every trouble that should not come upon the community, we sound the alarm for it, except for too much rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה and backs it up with a ברייתא. It sets up the question of why too much rain is left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is broad: any public trouble gets an alarm. There is one exception, too much rain. The next steps will explain why rain is treated differently.
steps.confusionAlert: 'שלא תבוא' literally means 'that should not come'. It is a polite way of talking about a trouble that might come, without saying it outright.

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: For every trouble that should not come upon the community, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה. Saying 'that should not come' is a gentle way to speak of a trouble that may come.

phrases.english: The רבנן taught:

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: For every trouble that should not come upon the community,
we sound the alarm for it, except for too much rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every public trouble gets an alarm, except too much rain.

steps.title: Why is too much rain left out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason that too much rain does not get an alarm.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why too much rain is the one exception. This sets up the answer of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Too much rain can do real damage, so it seems strange not to pray about it. The גמרא wants the logic behind the exception.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason of the exception in step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is too much rain the one trouble we do not sound the alarm for?

steps.title: We do not pray against too much good
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that rain is a good thing, and we do not pray to stop an excess of good.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Because we do not pray over too much good.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question: rain is a blessing, and we do not pray to stop a blessing even when there is a lot of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that rain belongs in the category of 'good', even when it falls in large amounts. Asking for a blessing to stop is not fitting, so no alarm is sounded.

keyTerms.meaning: Too much good, an excess of blessing

phrases.english: רבי יוחנן said:

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מִתְפַּלְּלִין עַל רוֹב הַטּוֹבָה.
phrases.english: Because we do not pray over too much good.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מִתְפַּלְּלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Rain is good, and we do not pray to stop an excess of good.

steps.title: A פסוק from מלאכי as the source
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן brings a פסוק about bringing the מעשר, which promises a blessing 'עד בלי די', as a source that we do not pray against too much good.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: From where do we know that we do not pray over too much good? As it says: 'Bring the whole מעשר into the storehouse...'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a source from a פסוק for the rule he just said. The key words are at the end of the פסוק, which the next step explains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in מלאכי promises a blessing so big it goes beyond 'enough'. If the תורה itself promises more than enough, we should not pray to stop it.

keyTerms.meaning: Tithe, a tenth of produce given away
And so on: the פסוק continues

phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן said:

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִין שֶׁאֵין מִתְפַּלְּלִין עַל רוֹב הַטּוֹבָה,
phrases.english: From where do we know that we do not pray over too much good?
As it says: 'Bring the whole מעשר'
phrases.notes: מלאכי 3:10. The פסוק ends with the words 'עד בלי די', which are the real proof.

phrases.english: 'into the storehouse, etc.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִין שֶׁאֵין מִתְפַּלְּלִין עַל רוֹב הַטּוֹבָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as the source for the reason in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we do not pray over too much good.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלאכי 3:10, which promises a blessing 'עד בלי די'.

steps.title: What does 'עד בלי די' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the words 'עד בלי די' at the end of the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'until there is no enough' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the unusual words 'עד בלי די' mean. This sets up רמי בר רב יוד's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depends on these words. The גמרא wants to know exactly how big the blessing is.

keyTerms.meaning: Until there is no 'enough': more than enough

phrases.english: What does 'until there is no enough' mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the key words of the פסוק quoted in step 29.

steps.title: So much blessing that your lips wear out
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר רב יוד explains: the blessing will be so great that your lips will wear out from saying 'enough'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר רב יוד said: Until your lips wear out from saying 'enough'.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר רב יוד explains the words: the word 'בלי' is read like 'יבלו', wear out. People will say 'enough' so many times that their lips get tired.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the blessing is far beyond what people need, and the פסוק still calls it a blessing. So even huge amounts of good are not something to pray against.

phrases.english: רמי בר רב יוד said:
Until your lips wear out
phrases.notes: He reads 'בלי' from the פסוק like 'יבלו', which means wearing out.

phrases.english: from saying 'enough'.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר רַב יוֹד: עַד שֶׁיִּבְלוּ שִׂפְתוֹתֵיכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The blessing will be so large that your lips wear out from saying 'enough'.
steps.whatToRemember: Rain is a blessing, and we do not pray to stop a blessing, even a huge one (מלאכי: 'עד בלי די').

steps.title: In the גולה, we do cry out over too much rain
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר רב יוד says that outside ארץ ישראל, in the גולה, we do sound the alarm over too much rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר רב יוד said: And in the גולה, we do sound the alarm over it.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר רב יוד adds an exception: the rule of not crying out over rain does not apply in the גולה. There, we do sound the alarm over too much rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule about not praying against too much good stays the same in general. But in the גולה, too much rain becomes a real danger, so it is treated like any other trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: The lands outside ארץ ישראל where Jews live (here, בבל)

phrases.english: רמי בר רב יוד said:
And in the גולה, we sound the alarm over it.
phrases.notes: 'It' means too much rain, from the ברייתא in step 26.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר רַב יוֹד: וּבַגּוֹלָה, מַתְרִיעִין עָלֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a place-based exception to the rule of step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the גולה, we sound the alarm over too much rain.

steps.title: The משמר asked the מעמד to pray for the גולה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רמי בר רב יוד: in a very rainy year, the משמר sent word to the מעמד to pray for their brothers in the גולה, so their houses would not become their graves.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: In a year with a lot of rain, the people of the משמר send to the people of the מעמד: Put your eyes on your brothers in the גולה, so that their houses do not become their graves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רמי בר רב יוד. It shows that people prayed about too much rain for the sake of the Jews in the גולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ארץ ישראל the rain was a blessing, but in the גולה houses could fall down from it. So they prayed for the people in the גולה, which proves that there too much rain counts as a trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא also teaches this: a support for the last statement
The group of כהנים serving that week in the בית המקדש
The group of ישראלים who stood and prayed alongside that week's service

steps.whatToRemember: No alarm over too much rain, because it is a blessing. But in the גולה, too much rain is dangerous, so we do cry out over it.

phrases.english: A ברייתא also teaches this:
A year whose rains are plentiful,
the people of the משמר send to the people of the מעמד:
Put your eyes on your brothers in the גולה,
so that their houses do not become their graves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the statement of רמי בר רב יוד in step 32.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that in the גולה we cry out over too much rain.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about the משמר asking the מעמד to pray for the people in the גולה in a rainy year.

steps.title: How much rain before we pray for it to stop?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר is asked how much rain must fall before people should pray for the rain to stop.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רבי אליעזר: How much rain has to fall before they should pray that it stop falling?
steps.whatsHappening: Students ask רבי אליעזר for the exact amount of rain that makes it right to pray for the rain to stop. The גמרא is setting up his answer, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we learned that there are times when it is proper to pray against too much rain. Now someone wants a measurement: at what point does rain go from a blessing to a danger worth praying about?

keyTerms.meaning: Up to what point? How much?

phrases.english: They asked Rabbi Eliezer:
How much must rain fall
until they should pray that it not fall anymore?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing that one may pray against excess rain in some situations, this step asks for the amount that triggers that prayer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The amount of rainfall at which it becomes proper to pray for the rain to stop.

steps.title: Enough to dip one's feet in water at קרן אפל
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר answers: enough rain that a person standing at קרן אפל could dip his feet in the water.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Enough that a person can stand at קרן אפל and dip his feet in the water.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר answers that the rain must be so much that a person standing at a place called קרן אפל could splash his feet in the water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is an exaggeration meant to describe an enormous flood. As the next steps show, קרן אפל is extremely high, so water reaching up there means a truly massive amount of rain. The point is that we pray against rain only when there is an overwhelming excess.

keyTerms.meaning: A place name, a very high cliff

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as a literal measurement. It is an exaggerated picture showing that only a huge flood calls for praying against rain.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Enough that a person stands at Keren Ophel
and dips his feet in the water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 34.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Enough rain that someone standing at קרן אפל could dip his feet in the water.

steps.title: A ברייתא says 'hands,' not 'feet'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: a ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר as saying 'his hands,' not 'his feet.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: 'his hands'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that a ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר differently, saying the person dips his 'hands' in the water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions of רבי אליעזר's words seem to clash. Hands and feet are not at the same height, so the measurement would change depending on which word he really said.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: "his hands"!
phrases.notes: The ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר saying the person dips his hands, not his feet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רבי אליעזר's answer in step 35.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording 'his feet' in רבי אליעזר's answer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא quotes him as saying 'his hands,' which contradicts the version saying 'his feet.'

steps.title: Feet as easily as hands
steps.stepSummary: The answer: when he said 'feet,' he meant as easily as hands, so the two versions fit together.
steps.simpleTranslation: I said 'his feet' meaning like his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in רבי אליעזר's voice: when he said 'feet,' he meant feet as easily as hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions are not arguing. The water must be high enough that the person can dip his feet just as easily as he could dip his hands. So both words are part of one picture.

phrases.english: I said "his feet" meaning like his hands.
phrases.notes: This is spoken as if רבי אליעזר himself is explaining what he meant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonizing two versions of the same statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Feet' and 'hands' seemed to be two different measurements.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Feet' means feet as easily as hands, so both versions describe the same amount of water.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה describes how tall קרן אפל is
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה says he saw קרן אפל, and an Arab riding a camel and holding a spear below it looked as small as a worm.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: I myself saw קרן אפל. An Arab was standing there, riding a camel and holding a spear in his hand, and he looked like a worm.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה tells what he saw: from קרן אפל, a man on a camel holding a spear looked as tiny as a worm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how enormously high קרן אפל is. It makes clear that רבי אליעזר's measurement describes an unbelievably huge flood, so praying against rain is only for extreme cases.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
I myself saw Keren Ophel,
where a certain Arab was standing
while riding a camel
and holding a spear in his hand,
and he looked like a worm.

steps.title: Rain 'in its season' means a moderate amount
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains 'I will give your rains in their season' as a moderate amount of rain, not too much and not too little, because too much rain ruins the land. It then begins a second explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'I will give your rains in their season' means the land will be neither drunk nor thirsty, but in between. Whenever the rains are too much, they turn the land to mud and it does not produce fruit. Another explanation:
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא explains that the blessing of rain 'in its season' is a balanced, moderate amount. At the very end, the גמרא is setting up a second explanation of the same פסוק, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land is pictured as a person: too much rain makes it 'drunk,' too little makes it 'thirsty.' Too much rain muddies the soil so nothing grows. This explains why excess rain is a real problem and fits the earlier discussion about praying against too much rain.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the true blessing of rain is balance. That is why too much rain can be a problem worth praying about.
